correctness.rationale: The ordered pair type records adjacency and each fresh third-vertex adjacency pattern. Last-round repetitions are already fixed by equality; a repeated second choice only needs the available neighbor/nonneighbor flags of the first vertex, which are projections of its pointed profile. Distinct sets of pointed profiles are separated by a rank-three sentence specifying a first vertex and exactly its possible pair types. For N≥8 in dimension ≥2, the union of two closed line-graph neighborhoods has size ≤4D−2<ND/2, giving 00. For intersecting root edges, separate-endpoint edges and a shared-endpoint third edge give the other patterns. For disjoint edges, failure of an exclusive pattern forces both endpoints of one edge to have both endpoints of the other as common neighbors and D=3; an adjacent pair in such a Hamming graph has at most one common neighbor. The 11 bit for disjoint root edges is exactly the existence of a joining edge; each anchor has a connected opposite edge in a coordinate square. An unconnected disjoint edge can always be made using two spare coordinates, or using a third value and two fresh values in the two nonbinary axes. With a binary and an order-q factor, binary-axis edges see all disjoint edges via a joining edge, whereas an order-q-axis edge has an unconnected opposite-row edge for q≥4. I independently enumerated all anchors and pair signatures in the nine representatives, including the prism exception (one W nonadjacency type only for the three-valued axis); replay: python3 /workspace/branches/independent-boundary-checks.py. The representative profiles are distinct and agree with the table. Class H has q² vertices with q≥4; for class I, d≥3 implies N≥8,D≥3, and two nonbinary factors give N≥9,D≥4. Together with the other table minima this gives the sharp within-family bound 16. Frozen scripts are finite supporting evidence, not the proof of the uniform classification.
